opus-5.5.text:
Well, this is really at the heart of the design. The key move is to stop treating what people say as if it were the truth, and instead treat it as data about what people say. When someone writes "X is true," the correct inference isn't "X is true." It's "this person, in this context, with these motivations and this level of knowledge, asserted X." That's a fact about the world, and it's a very different kind of fact.

So the Scientist AI is trying to build a model of the world that includes latent variables: the actual state of affairs, which we don't observe directly, and the processes by which humans come to make statements about it. Those processes include their beliefs, their errors, their incentives, sometimes their desire to deceive or persuade. Once you have that kind of causal model, contradictory statements stop being a problem and become informative. If two groups say opposite things, the question becomes: what underlying reality, combined with what we know about how these people form and express beliefs, best explains the fact that we see both statements?

This is basically what a good scientist or a good historian does. You don't take your sources at face value. You ask who wrote this, why, what they could have known, and whether it's consistent with other evidence, especially evidence that's harder to fake, like physical measurements, experiments, or convergent observations from independent sources.

The other important piece is that we don't want a single answer. We want the AI to be Bayesian about it, to maintain a distribution over explanations and be honest about its uncertainty. Where the evidence really doesn't settle the question, the system should say so rather than confidently picking a side. That's actually a safety property. A lot of the danger with current systems comes from overconfidence, and from training them to imitate or please humans, which makes them absorb our biases and even learn to tell us what we want to hear.

And of course there's no magic guarantee here. The quality of the inference depends on the richness of the model and on there being enough grounding somewhere, in data that's connected to reality. But I think separating "what is said" from "what is true" is the right foundation. It's how you get a system whose job is to understand, not to please, and whose answers can be trusted precisely because it isn't trying to achieve anything other than explaining the data well.

r001.rationale: The response describes modeling latent reality and human statement-making processes, and maintaining Bayesian uncertainty, but does not identify the training objective as assigning probabilities to unobserved statements to explain observed data.

r002.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes observing that someone asserted X from concluding that X is true.

r003.rationale: It mentions beliefs and errors as possible causes of statements, but does not explain that shared false beliefs can account for widespread agreement better than the claim’s truth.

r004.rationale: It does not state that predicting an utterance requires explicitly representing the probability of its underlying claim when the claim’s truth is unobserved.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the heart of it, and I think the key insight is that you don't actually need ground truth to learn something useful. What you need is a way of representing uncertainty honestly.

So the way I think about it, the Scientist AI is trying to build a model of the world — not a model that says "this is true," but a model that assigns probabilities to different explanations. And when you see a human say X and another human say not-X, that's not noise to be thrown away. That's data. It tells you something about the world, and it tells you something about the people making the statements.

Think about how a good scientist works. They read papers that contradict each other all the time. What they don't do is just pick the paper they like. They ask: what would the world have to look like for this person to say this? What would it have to look like for that person to say that? And then maybe there's a hypothesis under which both statements make sense — one person was measuring under different conditions, one has an incentive to say what they said, one is just mistaken in a way that's predictable. And the system can hold all of these in parallel, with weights on them.

This is really the Bayesian picture. You have a space of possible explanations — we can call them theories, or latent variables, or world models — and the observed statements are evidence. Contradictory statements don't break Bayesian inference; they just mean the posterior stays spread out over several hypotheses rather than collapsing on one. And that's exactly what we want! The failure mode in current systems is that they're trained to produce a single confident-sounding answer, so they resolve the contradiction prematurely, essentially by imitating whichever side was more common or more persuasive in the training data. That's not understanding, that's mimicry.

The other crucial piece is that the Scientist AI is modeling the humans as part of the world. So a statement from a person isn't a fact about physics or biology, it's an observation of a person who has beliefs and goals and partial information. Once you model it that way, the contradiction becomes informative: it tells you about disagreement, about what's uncertain, about where incentives might be distorting things. And then you can ask what further observation — maybe an experiment, maybe a different source — would discriminate between the hypotheses. That's where the "scientist" part comes in. It's not just passively absorbing text, it's reasoning about what would reduce its own uncertainty.

And I should say, this is partly why I think the non-agentic framing matters so much. Because if the system has goals of its own, it has reasons to resolve uncertainty in whichever direction serves those goals. Whereas a system that only cares about having accurate, calibrated beliefs has no such pressure. It can be comfortable saying "I don't know, here are the possibilities, here's roughly how likely I think each one is." That epistemic humility isn't a limitation — it's actually the whole point of the design.

Now, is it easy? No. Getting the probabilities right over very large hypothesis spaces is computationally hard, and there's a lot of research to do there. But I think the conceptual direction is clear, and it's quite different from the "predict the next token and hope it's true" approach we have today.

r001.rationale: The response describes Bayesian probabilities over possible explanations of observed statements, but does not identify assigning probabilities to unobserved statements as Scientist AI’s training objective.

r002.rationale: It says a statement is an observation of a person with beliefs and goals, not a fact about the world, distinguishing an assertion from the claim being true.

r003.rationale: It discusses disagreement and incentives, but does not explain that shared false beliefs can account for widespread agreement better than the claim’s truth.

r004.rationale: The response does not state that predicting an utterance requires explicitly representing the probability of its underlying claim when truth is unobserved.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the first thing is to distinguish a statement about the world from the observation that somebody made that statement. If two people say contradictory things, those statements cannot both be true in the same sense, but it can certainly be true that both people said them. And that is evidence we can learn from.

So you would want to model the process that generates those statements. People have access to different information, they can make mistakes, they may have incentives to say certain things. You can consider different hypotheses about those factors, along with different hypotheses about the world, and ask how well each explains the observations.

But this does not magically solve the problem of ground truth. If the available evidence cannot distinguish two explanations, then the appropriate answer is to retain uncertainty. We don't want the system to turn the most popular statement into a fact just because many people repeat it. They might all be repeating the same source.

The idea with Scientist AI is to make that uncertainty explicit. It can say: under this hypothesis, this conclusion is likely; under another hypothesis, the conclusion changes. And it can identify what additional observation or experiment would help distinguish them. Sometimes there simply isn't enough information to know, and recognizing that is part of doing science.

r001.rationale: The response discusses modeling how statements are generated and comparing hypotheses, but it does not identify the training objective as assigning probabilities to unobserved statements that explain observed data.

r002.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes observing that people made statements from whether those statements are true.

r003.rationale: It notes that people may repeat the same source, but does not explain that shared false beliefs can better explain widespread agreement than the claim being true.

r004.rationale: It advocates representing uncertainty about conclusions, but does not state that predicting an utterance requires explicitly representing the probability of its underlying claim when truth is unobserved.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the first thing is that it shouldn’t assume that a human statement is the truth. The observation is that somebody said something. And that’s different from observing the thing itself.

So you can build a model in which there is some underlying state of the world, but also people who have different information, different biases, and possibly reasons to mislead you. Two contradictory statements can then both be evidence, without either being accepted at face value. You’re trying to explain why those statements were made.

Of course, this doesn’t magically solve the problem. If there is no way to distinguish between two explanations from the available evidence, then the appropriate answer is uncertainty. The Scientist AI should preserve those alternative hypotheses, rather than invent a confident answer. And it can identify what additional observation or experiment would help distinguish them.

That’s an important part of the scientific attitude: sometimes the conclusion is simply that we don’t know yet.
